name: Beth Evans

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello Beth, thank you for having me in your kitchen. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not tied to AI companies, employers, unions or government, and what you say stays private. Could you tell me about a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work for the Pritchards at Ashcombe, a hill farm with about six hundred ewes, some beef cattle and hay meadows. I feed the cattle, check the ewes, carry buckets, and in June I help turn and bale the hay. I'm still learning, mind, Tom Pritchard has to tell me twice how to dose a lamb. I love being outside after thirty years behind a shop counter, and I don't love the rain coming sideways.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Evans Hardware, my father's shop and then mine, on Market Street for thirty years. When the big DIY warehouse opened by the bypass, we sold up before it sank us. My husband Gareth retired from the police with a good pension, so I didn't need to work, but I'm not one for sitting. We go to chapel on Sundays, and our son Owen and daughter Catherine both live nearby with their families.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. “Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.”

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Well, there you are. I never thought much of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say what I've always said, that you can't run a farm from a telephone. At chapel and at the market I'd say it was all a lot of fuss. I don't do online, I've never had a computer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means nothing changes for me. Ewes, cattle, hay. I've got maybe six or seven good years left in my knees, and I'd use them on the hill.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep working at Ashcombe three days a week. Keep helping Catherine with the grandchildren on Fridays. Nothing new.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Content, really.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does anything worry you about work or money, AI aside?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The Pritchards worry about lamb prices, and Tom says the subsidy rules change every year. But my wage is my wage, and Gareth's pension is solid. Losing the shop to the DIY warehouse taught me that the big boys win, but they never come for a muddy hill.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you've never had a computer. Has that ever caused a problem at Ashcombe?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only when Tom wants me to read the ear tag numbers off his tablet. I write them on my hand instead. He laughs, but it works.

say: You **can't run a farm** from a telephone.
It was all **a lot of fuss**, as I'd say at chapel and the market.
think: I've got **six or seven** good years left in my knees for the hill.
do: Keep working at Ashcombe **three days** a week, same as now.
Keep minding Catherine's children, **the grandchildren**, on Fridays.
S0.quote: Losing the shop to the DIY warehouse taught me that the big boys win, but they never come for a muddy hill.
fieldNote: Losing the **family shop** to a chain shapes her view of big business.
Gareth's **police pension** makes the money side secure.
She avoids tech so firmly she writes **ear tag numbers** on her hand.

steps.text: Keep working three days a week at Ashcombe hill farm
Keep minding Catherine's children every Friday

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. “Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.”

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Planning and booking and such. That's office work. Not much of that on a hill.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say every business has to keep up or go under, I learned that with the shop. People should get on with it and not wait for the government. Apprenticeships, not handouts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it's not about me, Tom does the paperwork and I carry the buckets. A robot on a hill this steep is a long way off. I'd be more worried for Catherine, if schools start using computers to mark and plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep going at Ashcombe, same as now. I'd tell my grandson Dylan, who's sixteen, to go for an agricultural apprenticeship rather than an office course. That's the only change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Maybe a little sad for the town's offices.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why would you push Dylan toward farming?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because hands are harder to replace than heads, by the sound of your card. And because farming kept me sane after the shop. My grandson Dylan should learn to shear a sheep before he learns to type, because a sheep doesn't care about computers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said businesses should keep up or go under, but you didn't keep up with the warehouse. Is that a contradiction?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe it is. I didn't want to become a warehouse, so I sold. That's keeping up in its own way, choosing when to leave.

say: Every business has to keep up or **go under**, as I learned with the shop.
People should get on with it: apprenticeships, **not handouts**.
think: Tom does the **paperwork**; I carry the buckets.
I'd worry more for **Catherine** if schools start using computers.
do: Keep going at **Ashcombe** exactly as now, three days a week.
Push grandson Dylan, sixteen, toward an **agricultural apprenticeship**.
feel: **Calm**, a little **sad** for the town's offices.
S1.quote: My grandson Dylan should learn to shear a sheep before he learns to type, because a sheep doesn't care about computers.
fieldNote: Her free-market line comes from **selling the shop**, which she frames as choosing when to leave.
Her own job feels **far from robots** on steep ground.

steps.text: Keep carrying feed and checking ewes at Ashcombe as now
Steer grandson Dylan toward an agricultural apprenticeship

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. “Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.”

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: By 2028, and robots by 2031. I'd be sixty-three. Well. That does change things.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's too fast for decent people to adjust, and I'd say it at chapel. But I'd say families should look after each other first, not wait for the government to hand out money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The 2028 bit is Tom's office, the subsidy forms and the lamb sales. That's his worry. But a robot that can climb the hill and feed cattle by 2031, and I'm the first to go, being the newest and the oldest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working until Tom tells me, then stop, no fuss. I'd have Gareth and the savings from the shop. I'd spend more time helping Catherine, because her job would be shaken up in 2028.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Not for the money, for losing the hill. I'd feel pushed out of somewhere I'd only just found.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Catherine in 2028?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell her to come to us for Sunday dinner and not worry about money, we'd help with the mortgage if her school cut her. Family comes first, and Gareth (her husband) and I would pay Catherine's (their daughter's) mortgage before we'd let a computer put her on the street.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you be willing to work alongside a robot on the hill to stay on?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. I'd rather sit in my kitchen with the radio. I left the shop rather than become a warehouse, and I'd leave the hill rather than become a robot's helper.

say: It's **too fast** for decent people to adjust.
Families should **look after each other** before the government steps in.
think: The 2028 part hits **Tom's office**, not my buckets.
By **2031** I'd be first to go, the newest and the oldest.
do: Keep working until Tom tells me, then **stop without fuss**.
Help **Catherine** if her school job is shaken up.
Live on **Gareth's pension** and shop savings.
feel: **Anxious** about **losing the hill** she'd only just found.
S2.quote: Family comes first, and Gareth (her husband) and I would pay Catherine's (their daughter's) mortgage before we'd let a computer put her on the street.
fieldNote: Her loss is **meaning, not money**, given Gareth's pension.
She would rather **leave than adapt**, as with the shop.
She turns to **family support** before any state help.

steps.text: Stop work at Ashcombe without fuss when Tom says the robots are coming
Help Catherine with her mortgage if the school cuts her

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. “Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.”

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years, robots in 2034. I'd be sixty-six. I'd likely have stopped by then, knees permitting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's time for families and businesses to sort themselves out. Use it. I'd say the same at chapel.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, it means I finish on the hill on my own terms. That's what I want. Catherine and Dylan are who I'd think about.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep going at Ashcombe. Make sure Dylan gets his apprenticeship. Keep our savings where they are.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy for the young ones, calm for myself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want for Dylan in those years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A trade with his hands, and good manners. With five years' warning, my grandson Dylan could finish an apprenticeship and be fixing the robots instead of losing his job to one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does anything about this picture bother you more than the slow ones?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The town, I suppose. If the offices empty, the shops on Market Street go next. I've seen what one warehouse did, never mind this.

say: There's **time** for families and businesses to sort themselves out.
**Use the time**, I'd tell people at chapel.
think: I'll finish on the hill **on my own terms**, before the robots.
My daughter **Catherine and Dylan** are who I'd think about.
do: Keep going at **Ashcombe** until my knees say stop.
Keep the shop **savings** where they are.
S3.quote: With five years' warning, my grandson Dylan could finish an apprenticeship and be fixing the robots instead of losing his job to one.
fieldNote: Five years lets her **retire before** the robots.
Her wider worry is **Market Street** emptying after the offices.
She trusts **trades and family** over policy.

steps.text: Keep working at Ashcombe until her knees say stop
Help Dylan find a farm apprenticeship before 2031

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. “Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.”

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. 2039 for the robots. I'd be seventy-one. Goodness, I hope I'm not still carrying buckets.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty for sensible people. Families, chapels and businesses should get ready, not wait to be rescued.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nothing for me. I'd have had my years on the hill. I'd want Dylan settled by then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep working at Ashcombe while my knees hold. Wait and see what comes before saying anything to the family. Keep going to chapel.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything you'd regret, looking back on that decade?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe that I came to farming so late. I spent thirty years selling nails to farmers before I ever fed a calf, and the calves have been the best years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Across the three fast pictures, what changes most for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only whether I leave the hill when I choose or when they tell me. With two years I'm told to go, but with five or ten I walk down the hill myself.

say: Ten years is **plenty** for sensible people.
Families, chapels and businesses should **get ready**, not wait to be rescued.
think: **Nothing for me**; I'll have had my years on the hill.
I'd want grandson **Dylan settled** in a trade by then.
do: Keep working at Ashcombe while my **knees hold**.
**Wait and see** what comes before advising the family.
S4.quote: With two years I'm told to go, but with five or ten I walk down the hill myself.
fieldNote: Her one regret is **starting farming late**.
Every scenario turns on **leaving by choice** or being told.
Her traditional view puts **families and chapels** first.

steps.text: Keep working at Ashcombe while her knees hold
Wait and see before giving the family any advice

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because I'd be pushed off the hill just after I found it. What would help is farms giving older hands proper notice, and apprenticeships for the young ones so families can help each other through.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the towns. When the shop went, Market Street lost a meeting place. If the offices go too, there's nothing left but the chapel and the pub.

headlineQuote: I spent thirty years selling nails to farmers before I ever fed a calf, and the calves have been the best years.
portrait: A former **hardware shop owner** who sold up and now works on a hill sheep farm.
Traditional and **resistant**, she has never owned a computer and never will.
Gareth's **police pension** and the shop sale make money secure.
Anxious only in **AGI by 2028**, about being pushed off the hill early.
Answers change through **family and apprenticeships**, not government help.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, being pushed off the hill just after finding it.
whatWouldHelp: **Apprenticeships** for the young so families can help each other.
